system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2135-10-01 14:54:00 to 2135-10-03 17:52:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, chronic systolic heart failure, and anoxic brain injury was admitted for evaluation of chest pain that occurred after coughing during a dialysis session. The pain was sharp, midline, and resolved spontaneously, differing from his prior cardiac pain. Workup showed no EKG changes, troponin levels were within his baseline, and imaging revealed no pulmonary edema or acute cardiac issues. The pain was determined to be musculoskeletal in origin, likely due to coughing from a viral illness. Hyperkalemia was noted but managed with dialysis. He remained hemodynamically stable, completed a dialysis session, and was discharged home with aspirin restarted and instructions to follow up with his specialists.
problems: Diabetes with renal manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I had bad stomach pain last night, mostly in the upper middle part. I also threw up once this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was the pain sharp or dull? Did it go anywhere else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was a dull ache, stayed in the middle. No radiation. But I did feel feverish at home yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a dry cough for about a week, but no chest pain or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I see you’re on dialysis. Did you have a session today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had dialysis earlier today before coming here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your blood pressure was high in the ER—193 over 94—but it came down to 174 over 80 after dialysis. We also saw your potassium was high at 6.2, so you got some IV meds to bring that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. I sometimes get high potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your abdomen because of the pain. It showed some thickening of the gallbladder wall, which can suggest inflammation—possibly cholecystitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cholecystitis? Like gallbladder infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But the scan didn’t show gallstones, so it’s not clear-cut. The ultrasound was also inconclusive. So we’re going to do a HIDA scan tomorrow to get more information.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. If it’s not cholecystitis, we won’t need surgery. We’re also considering other causes like gastritis or your diabetes affecting stomach emptying—gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had gastroparesis before. But I’m already on pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll keep that. Since you’re allergic to Reglan, we can’t use that. But we’ve given you Zofran for nausea, and you haven’t vomited since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not since this morning. The pain’s also better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ve started antibiotics just in case—levofloxacin and flagyl—until we rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I hope the scan helps figure it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the HIDA scan yesterday. It didn’t show cholecystitis, which is good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. So it’s not my gallbladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely, no. But the scan showed delayed emptying of the tracer into your small bowel. That could mean a spasm in the sphincter of Oddi—sort of a valve that controls bile flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what does that mean for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might explain your pain and nausea. We’ve stopped the antibiotics since there’s no infection. Your symptoms are improving, and you’re not running a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it could be related to my diabetes or just a temporary spasm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both are possible. We’re also seeing some elevated liver enzymes—alkaline phosphatase and GGT—which could tie into this. But your liver function is otherwise normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had high alk phos before. It’s usually around 150 to 200.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, and it was 320 on admission but is coming down. We don’t have a full explanation, but it may be related to the sphincter issue. We’ve ordered hepatitis tests just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. No signs of serious liver disease. We’ll follow up in the GI clinic in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. No pain, no nausea. Still coughing a little, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your lungs have some mild wheezing, but no pneumonia. The cough might be from a mild viral illness, especially with your dry cough and recent fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I didn’t feel well for a couple days before coming in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re planning to discharge you today. Your symptoms are gone, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. So what was the cause?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t have a single clear cause, but it’s likely a mix—possibly a viral illness or gastritis, maybe worsened by your diabetes or the sphincter spasm. No infection was found, so we stopped antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with the same medications. No changes. Keep taking your insulin, pantoprazole, and phenytoin. Follow up with GI in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have fever, severe pain, or vomiting. Otherwise, you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Someone will help you home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of type 1 diabetes, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, chronic systolic heart failure, and seizure disorder was admitted for epigastric abdominal pain and vomiting. Initial imaging showed gallbladder wall thickening concerning for cholecystitis, prompting treatment with antibiotics. A HIDA scan ruled out acute cholecystitis but revealed delayed tracer emptying, suggestive of sphincter of Oddi spasm. Symptoms improved with conservative management and anti-nausea medication. Elevated liver enzymes were noted but attributed to chronic changes; hepatitis workup was initiated. The patient remained afebrile, with resolution of symptoms, and was discharged home on unchanged medications with follow-up in gastroenterology.
